query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of multi‐element, near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions is primarily governed by lattice distortion–induced sluggish diffusion. This sluggish diffusion, arising from atomic size mismatches and high configurational entropy, kinetically impedes elemental segregation and phase separation despite thermodynamic drives toward ordering.
generation.material_initial_state: Near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles fabricated via either thermal shock or electrodeposition methods, exhibiting a uniform, disordered solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: (1) HEA nanoparticles containing five or more elements to maximize lattice distortion effects, and (2) binary or limited multicomponent alloy nanoparticles with a similar average noble metal content but reduced compositional complexity. This controlled variation isolates the effect of lattice distortion and mixing entropy on diffusion and stability.
generation.conditions: Expose both nanoparticle sets to service-relevant temperatures for catalytic operation (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric use (473–1923 K) under identical inert (or controlled) atmospheres, ensuring that substrate and environmental conditions do not vary between samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion induced by the large atomic size mismatches and random mixing in the HEA nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: In the multi-element nanoparticles, high configurational entropy and significant lattice distortions increase the activation energy for atomic diffusion, thereby retarding atom mobility. This sluggish diffusion prevents the atoms from rearranging into segregated or ordered phases, maintaining the homogeneous alloy structure even under high-temperature stress. In contrast, binary or lower-order alloys, with less lattice distortion, permit faster diffusion, leading to phase separation or elemental segregation under the same conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the binary or less complex alloy controls, the HEA nanoparticles will exhibit lower measured diffusion coefficients, maintain a more homogeneous elemental distribution, and show minimal morphological changes and phase separations after high-temperature exposure. These effects should be observable as a sustained catalytic or thermoelectric performance and structural integrity relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Binary or limited multicomponent alloy nanoparticles with similar noble-metal content but lower mixing entropy and lattice distortion.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies when synthesis produces uniformly mixed nanoparticles without significant substrate or support-induced stabilization. It may not hold under conditions where extreme oxidizing environments or temperatures far outside the specified ranges induce failure modes not mitigated by lattice distortion effects.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports a role for sluggish diffusion due to lattice distortion in enhancing stability, quantitative differences in diffusion rates and the relative impact compared to other factors (such as support interactions) remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two nanoparticle samples: one set of near-equiatomic HEA nanoparticles (e.g., CoNiCuRuPd) and a control set of binary or lower-order alloy nanoparticles with comparable noble-metal content and similar size distributions. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature treatments (using temperatures appropriate for catalytic and thermoelectric applications) in an inert atmosphere for a fixed period. Characterize the samples before and after treatment using in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and elemental mapping (e.g., via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy or ICP-OES).
measurements: Atomic diffusion coefficients (e.g., via in situ TEM studies)
Morphological changes (particle size distribution and shape analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA nanoparticles do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in atomic diffusion rates, or if they show similar or greater levels of elemental segregation, phase transformation, or morphological coarsening compared to the binary control under identical high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion–induced sluggish diffusion governs their stability will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We have developed advanced ammonia decomposition catalysts based on high-entropy alloys made of earth-abundant elements. The HEA CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles enabled robust tuning of the Co/Mo ratio and breaking the miscibility limitation in conventional bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts. These novel catalysts achieved significantly enhanced catalytic activities and stabilities, with the improvement factors exceeding 20 times as compared to precious metal Ru, and even more so versus conventional Co-Mo catalysts. Their catalytic activities and kinetics were further found to exhibit a volcano-type behavior independent of the Co/Mo ratio, which was successfully interpreted by using the nitrogen adsorption energy as the descriptor and a mixed surface site mechanism derived from atomistic modeling. The robust tunability of alloy composition and surface adsorption property demonstrated on the HEA catalysts indicate great potential for their implementation in practical reactors with the catalytic performance optimized under various reaction conditions.

The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). To further verify the structural stability, we performed MD simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient of the Ru element in Ru-5 MEA and compared it with Ru in a binary Ru-Ni alloy. In an effort to better understand the high robustness of the HEA NPs, theoretical investigations were conducted employing cluster models. DFT calculations demonstrated that the cohesive energy (Ec) of a Co16Ni15Cu16Ru16Pd16 HEA cluster was −3.92 eV, which was higher than the value of −3.09 eV for a Pd79 cluster (Fig. 7a). Combining these data with molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, diffusion coefficients (D) were determined at 900 K after 0.1 ps (Supplementary Fig. 18). The results demonstrated that the D values of all metals in a Co16Ni15Cu16Ru16Pd16 HEA cluster were lower than those for the corresponding monometallic clusters (Co79, Cu79, Ni79, Ru79, or Pd79) (Fig. 7b). As an example, the D for Pd in a Co16Ni16Cu15Ru16Pd16 HEA cluster was calculated to be 1.31 × 10−5 m2/s, and so was approximately one-third lower than the value of 3.43 × 10−5 m2/s for a Pd79 cluster. These results provide further evidence that sluggish diffusion in the HEA NPs, originating from the mixing of multiple elements and from lattice distortion effects, contributed significantly to the high resistance of the HEA NPs against the undesired irreversible agglomeration and radiation damage process.
